assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made a single superconducting artificial atom strongly coupled to a single microwave photon, giving dispersive readout, cavity-mediated gates and bus coupling. It is the architecture underlying essentially all superconducting quantum processors and a whole field of microwave quantum optics. It is original, clear and demonstrably far-reaching; the strong-coupling regime showed a new, controllable regime of light-matter interaction on a chip.
assessment.attribution: Theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf, 2004) and first experiment (Wallraff et al., 2004, Yale) are tightly linked. Schoelkopf and Wallraff led the experimental realisation and its development; Girvin is the leading theoretical architect with Blais. Four credited names but the prize allows three, so one of the Girvin/Blais theory pair is left out, which is a real allocation difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Replicated and extended by dozens of laboratories over two decades, interpretation stable, and recognition is timely. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is adjacent, so the committee must judge that this is a distinct discovery rather than a follow-on; I regard it as distinct (light-matter coupling versus tunnelling and quantisation in a circuit).
uncertainties: I work in this field and direct a national programme built on this architecture, so my judgement may be biased and recusal rules might apply.
Allocation between Blais and Girvin on the theory side is unresolved.
Close adjacency to the 2025 prize may weigh against it in committee.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and the experimental realisation of ion-trap quantum logic and entanglement of many ions made quantum computation a concrete physical proposal. Originality is high, the proposal was specific and testable, and it seeded ion-trap quantum computing and simulation. Wineland's 2012 prize recognised ion control, so this recognises the quantum-computing architecture proper.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the clear theoretical originators of the 1995 gate proposal. Blatt is the leading experimentalist who realised gates, entanglement and scaling in the Innsbruck group; Wineland (already a laureate) and Monroe/Kielpinski also contributed, and the credit set is not uncontroversially complete.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent groups with high-fidelity gates, and commercial systems exist. Timely; the discovery is mature, though scalable fault-tolerant machines remain ahead.
uncertainties: Overlap in credit with Wineland's earlier prize and with other experimental groups such as Monroe's.
Partly an enabling technology claim; I need to be careful to reward the discovery rather than the application.
Cirac and Zoller also appear under a separate optical-lattice and Rydberg candidate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and fault-tolerant computation showed that quantum information can in principle be protected against decoherence, answering the central objection to quantum computers. Shor's code and Steane's codes, with Kitaev's topological codes and fault-tolerance ideas, form the conceptual basis of the whole experimental programme now being pursued on chips. Deep and lasting, though it is more theoretical computer science and information theory than physics discovery.
assessment.attribution: Shor (first code, 1995), Steane (CSS codes) and Kitaev (toric code, anyonic fault tolerance) are decisive; Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Preskill, Aharonov and Ben-Or also made decisive contributions, so the credit is genuinely diffuse and any three-person set is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations of below-threshold logical qubits have appeared only recently (superconducting and neutral-atom platforms), so the physical validation of the idea is just maturing. The theory is stable but the physics-prize relevance is arguably still early.
uncertainties: Whether the Physics committee considers this a physics discovery rather than computer science.
Fuzzy attribution among many contributors.
Experimental validation of scalable fault tolerance is still incomplete.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics and quantum acoustics brought mechanical oscillators to their quantum ground state, enabled sideband cooling, and showed quantum control of mechanical objects including entanglement and coupling to superconducting qubits. It extends the quantum regime to macroscopic mass, closely connected to the 2025 theme, and it is clean physics that opened a new regime.
assessment.attribution: Cleland (first quantum ground-state mechanical resonator with a qubit, 2010), Kippenberg (radiation-pressure cooling, strong coupling) and Aspelmeyer (quantum optomechanics) are central; O'Connell, Teufel, Lehnert, Painter and Schwab also did decisive work, so the set is arbitrary in part.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced in several platforms and interpretation is stable, but the field is still developing and its transformative applications and tests of fundamental physics are not yet realised. Recognition is somewhat early.
uncertainties: Credit is spread among at least six strong groups.
Impact beyond the field is still modest compared with qubit architectures.
I know the quantum-acoustics literature personally, as I co-authored related work, so judgement may be biased.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, from Katori's magic-wavelength proposal onward, reached 10^-18 fractional uncertainty and enable new tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. The discovery is clean, quantitative and robust, and the precision-measurement field is a classical recipient area for the prize, building on the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength scheme and demonstrated the first clock, and Ye pushed the system to record precision and many-body (spin-exchange) effects. A two-person split is natural, though Lemonde, Kimble, Hollberg and others made contributions.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories reproduce and compare clocks, interpretation is stable, and timing is right, especially with plans to redefine the second.
uncertainties: Overlap with the earlier Hall and Hansch frequency-comb prize and Ye's role there.
Whether a redefinition of the second will be seen as the right moment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices (the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and later many-body physics) gave a controllable realisation of Hubbard-type models and a new window onto strongly correlated matter. It is original and foundational, though much of the impact is as a platform.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch et al.) provided the proposal, Bloch and Greiner the experiments, including the Mott transition and later quantum gas microscopes. Dalibard and Cirac are also credited; credit is dense and the set is contestable, and Greiner is part of the Hulet-Bloch-Greiner lineage.
assessment.maturity: Highly reproduced and mature. Still, the long-promised solutions to hard many-body problems are only partly realised, so I weigh the platform-versus-discovery balance with some caution.
uncertainties: Credit is broad, and Zoller's name appears on other candidates, so a set with Zoller twice may be undesirable.
Overlap with ion-trap and neutral-atom candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction and observation of the time-reversal-invariant quantum spin Hall state and topological insulators created a new classification of electronic phases and a huge research programme. It is original and very important, though outside my own area, so I defer partly to colleagues.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele provided the theoretical prediction; Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang's proposal and Molenkamp's HgTe experiment (König et al., 2007) confirmed it. Credit for the three-dimensional case (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore and Balents; Hasan, Cava) is not captured, so attribution is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed across many materials, though the original practical hopes for dissipationless transport have been limited.
uncertainties: Missing 3D topological insulator contributors and the BHZ proposal.
Outside my expertise and I defer to condensed-matter colleagues.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade and programmable neutral-atom arrays have enabled controllable many-body quantum simulation, high-fidelity gates and early quantum computing demonstrations. The science is exciting and fast-moving, and it has been tested against the questions that matter for quantum technology.
assessment.attribution: Lukin, Browaeys and Saffman carried out decisive experimental work; Zoller (with Jaksch et al.) proposed the blockade, and Weiss, Endres and Bernien also contributed. The credit is dispersed over a very young field.
assessment.maturity: Still strongly evolving, and some key claims such as large-scale error-corrected computation have not matured; this is a premature candidate.
uncertainties: Probably premature.
Credit has not stabilised and overlaps with the Zoller trapped-ion and lattice candidates.
